title: Chapter 27: Ocean Relief, Temperature and Salinity

blocks.content: The oceans cover about 71% of the Earth's surface and contain nearly 97% of the planet’s water. They play a crucial role in regulating climate, supporting biodiversity, influencing weather systems, and sustaining human livelihoods. Understanding ocean relief, temperature, and salinity is fundamental to mastering physical geography because these factors control ocean circulation, marine ecosystems, and global heat distribution.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Ocean relief shapes depth variations through tectonic activity, volcanism, and sediment deposition.
Ocean temperature varies vertically across three zones: Surface Zone, Thermocline, and Deep Zone.
Average ocean salinity is 35‰, reaching its highest levels in subtropical regions due to high evaporation.
Seawater density is determined by temperature and salinity, driving deep ocean thermohaline circulation.

blocks.content: Ocean relief refers to the variation in depth and shape of the ocean floor. Just like continents have mountains and plains, the ocean floor has diverse landforms formed by tectonic activity, volcanism, and sediment deposition.
Major Divisions of Ocean Floor Major Divisions of Ocean Floor

cells: Gently sloping submerged extension of continents; average depth 0–200 m. Rich in marine life and major fishing zones. Petroleum extraction is common here.
Steep descent from shelf to deep ocean floor; marks the true boundary of continents.
Gentle incline formed by sediments deposited at the base of the slope.
Extremely flat and deep regions (3000–6000 m); among the smoothest surfaces on Earth.
Deepest parts of oceans formed at subduction zones; e.g., Mariana Trench (~11,000 m).
Underwater mountain chains formed due to seafloor spreading; volcanically active.
Submerged volcanic mountains that do not reach the surface.
Flat-topped seamounts eroded by waves before subsiding.

blocks.content: Ocean temperature varies both horizontally and vertically. Since water has high heat capacity, oceans act as thermal reservoirs, moderating global climate.

cells: Equatorial waters are warmer than polar waters.
Warm currents raise temperatures; cold currents lower them.

blocks.content: • Surface Zone – Warm due to solar radiation.
Temperature and salinity together control seawater density, which drives thermohaline circulation — often called the global ocean conveyor belt.
• Thermocline – Rapid temperature decrease with depth.
• Deep Zone – Very cold and stable (around 0–3°C).
The thermocline acts as a barrier preventing mixing between warm surface water and cold deep water.
Salinity refers to the concentration of dissolved salts in seawater, usually expressed in parts per thousand (‰). The average ocean salinity is about 35‰.

rows: Acts as a barrier preventing mixing between surface and deep water
Deepest layer containing cold, dense ocean water

blocks.content: • Highest in subtropical regions due to high evaporation.
• Lower near the equator because of heavy rainfall.
• Very low in polar regions due to melting ice.
Salinity generally decreases with depth and becomes relatively stable in deeper layers.
Temperature and salinity together control seawater density, which drives thermohaline circulation — often called the global ocean conveyor belt.

items: Continental shelf is the richest fishing zone, whereas Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean point.
The thermocline layer exhibits a rapid decline in temperature and acts as a barrier preventing water layer mixing.
Salinity is highest in subtropical regions due to high evaporation, lower near the equator, and lowest in polar regions.
Thermohaline circulation is driven by density differences resulting from temperature and salinity variations.

blocks.content: • Thermohaline Circulation – Deep ocean movement driven by density differences.
• Halocline – Layer with rapid salinity change.
• Upwelling – Rising of nutrient-rich cold water supporting fisheries.
• El Niño disrupts normal ocean temperature patterns.

• Continental shelf is the richest fishing zone.
• Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean point.
